Hirschsprung's disease is a disorder in which nerve cells that help control muscles in the colon don't migrate normally during fetal development. This results in parts of the colon without nerves and without the ability to pull together (contract) to push food out of the body. Because of this, stool stays in the colon too long and the body's immune system responds by forming swollen tissues, called abscesses, which can cause holes or tears in the colon. It usually causes symptoms in the first year of life, but may present at any age up to about 50 years. It is more common in males than females. PGHS has a cylo-oxygenase domain and a peroxidase domain. Ibuprofen acts as a reversible competitive inhibitor of the COX domain. Competitive inhibitors bind directly to the active site of the enzymes and are able to displace the substrate for the reaction. This means that the enzyme has a lower affinity for the substrate and therefore less product is formed. Non-competitive inhibitors do not bind directly to the active site of the enzyme but instead cause changes in the shape of it. This means they are often allosteric inhibitors which change the shape of the enzyme at sites other than the active site. This means that there is no effect on Km (affinity for substrate) and Vmax (maximum rate of reaction). Instead, the enzyme has a lower catalytic activity.  NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are competitive inhibitors of COX and so have similar effects to aspirin, which is also a competitive inhibitor of COX. Paracetamol, however, works by inhibiting the peroxidase domain of PGHS which is why it has different side effects to NSAIDs. It only inhibits one of two products of PGHS and so still allows production of prostaglandins with pain-relieving properties. This means that paracetamol takes longer to work than NSAIDs but its effects last longer. Paracetamol also does not have the same anti-inflammatory effects as NSAIDs. Aspirin and ibuprofen both irreversibly inhibit COX whereas paracetamol does not. This is because the NSAIDs are designed to be slow to be broken down by enzymes in the body so that they stay in the system for long enough to have their desired effect. Whereas paracetamol is designed to be quickly broken down by the body's enzymes so that any excess passes through the kidneys into urine without building up in the system. This is why NSAIDs are associated with more side effects than paracetamol.  I made this question quite difficult for myself! Urea breath test can be used to diagnose H pylori infection. Urea is broken down into ammonia which has a pungent smell. Ammonia then diffuses into the circulation where it binds to plasma albumin. When this occurs it loses its volatility and cannot be exhaled therefore if urea is being exhaled via the breath this suggests the presence of H pylori.  Urea can also accumulate in AKI and cause symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, confusion and asterixis (tremor). This is because urea can cross the blood brain barrier and is highly neurotoxic. It causes swelling of the brain and can lead to coma.  High levels of potassium can also cause similar symptoms however would not be the most likely answer.  Other signs of urea accumulation are hypotension due to volume overload (high circulating volumes of urea), oliguria (low urine output) and acidosis due to production of ammonia (which dissociates to give ammonium and hydrogen ions).  Creatinine is produced from creatine phosphate and is not normally filtered by the kidneys. Therefore elevated levels indicate impaired kidney function.  Lactic acid does not relate to renal failure. It is produced when there is a lack of oxygen supply to cells and is associated with shock.  Calcium can also cause similar symptoms but is less likely than urea. It is involved in excitability and can cause tetany (seizures). However in severe states it can cause coma.   Source: Case 12 Nephrotic syndrome lecture. Golfer's elbow refers to inflammation of the tendons that connect the forearm to the elbow, caused by overuse of the muscles of your forearm. Inflammation causes pain and tenderness, making it difficult to use your arm. Golfer's elbow occurs when tendons in your forearm are overworked, usually from repetitive movements of the wrist and arm. Golfer's elbow often occurs in people who engage in activities that require using the flexor muscles of the forearm, such as painting, hammering, pitching baseball and playing golf. Golfer's elbow primarily affects those who play sports regularly or perform physical labor (such as plumbing or carpentry). Golfer's elbow may also occur in people whose jobs require forceful use of their arms, especially in unnatural positions. Pain associated with golfer's elbow typically radiates from the elbow into the forearm. The pain may be sharp and stabbing at first but eventually becomes more dull and aching. The symptoms of golfer's elbow vary depending on the severity of the injury and your level of activity. Symptoms include: Pain and tenderness near the elbow that increases with use of the armWeakness in the hand and wristMuscle stiffnessWarmth and redness around the affected area Swelling. Treatment: Rest, ice and anti-inflammatory medications are often used to treat golfer's elbow. Cortisone injections may be used to relieve pain if rest and other measures aren't effective. If these treatments don't help, surgery to release the tendon may be necessary.  The medial epicondyle is the bony prominence on the inside of the elbow that is felt when flexing the hand. This is known as golfer's elbow. It is the point where the common tendinous ring of flexor muscles of the forearm attaches to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Arteriosclerosis is the hardening and thickening of the walls of the arteries, usually without any change in lumen size. It is caused by deposition of collagen and other connective tissue within the tunica media. It is often associated with hypertension as the vessels become stiffer and less compliant. Atherosclerosis is the process of disease in which fatty deposits build up inside the blood vessels. These deposits are called plaques and are made up of cholesterol, fat, and other cells. Over time, these plaques can grow large enough to block the blood vessels and cause serious problems like heart attacks or strokes.  Atherosclerosis is one type of cardiovascular disease. Other types include coronary heart disease, peripheral vascular disease, and cerebrovascular disease. Cardiovascular diseases are some of the leading causes of death worldwide. They kill more people each year than any other kind of disease. There are many risk factors for cardiovascular disease including high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, obesity, and lack of exercise. Some people have genetic conditions that make them more likely to develop cardiovascular disease at an early age. Others may have no known risk factors but still develop the condition later in life. If you think you might be at risk for cardiovascular disease, talk to your doctor about getting screened regularly so that treatment can start early if needed! Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a drug class that provides analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects. The most widely used NSAIDs are ibuprofen (e.g., Advil), naproxen sodium (e.g., Aleve), and aspirin. All NSAIDs inhibit the activity of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes. COX-1 produces prostaglandins involved in renal, hepatic, and intestinal physiology; COX-2 produces prostaglandins involved in inflammation. Blocking COX-1 inhibits prostaglandin production, reducing inflammation but also interfering with normal cell function. Selective COX-2 inhibitors have been developed to address this problem by only inhibiting the COX-2 enzyme. Tylenol (acetaminophen) is not an NSAID because it does not affect the COX enzymes. Instead, it acts primarily on peripheral opioid receptors and central NMDA glutamate receptors. 80% of IgG from mother passes into baby. Stays in the blood for a while but is then transferred to breast milk where it stays at high levels for protection (in particular against measles). It's also the only antibody that can cross the blood brain barrier. Note that IgM is initially produced during viral infection (as pro-IgM) as this is needed for the complement system as it binds more effectively. However, after somatic hypermutation, IgM is no longer produced. It is IgG that is high affinity and long lived. Also, IgA is found in mucosal areas. All these features are beneficial for protecting a baby. Therefore, IgG is the only antibody to cross the placenta and therefore is found in high concentrations in newborns. This means that if a baby was born with a low IgG concentration, they would be less protected than others. This could lead to them getting a virus or bacterial infection which they wouldn’t usually get. Immunocompromised patients may have a lowered ability to produce IgG which is why they are advised to have an injection every year to help boost their immunity. The pH and BE indicate that this patient has acidosis - as he is breathing oxygen therapy it could be respiratory or metabolic in origin.The PaO2 is low indicating poor perfusion and therefore the problem is not purely respiratory.Therefore the ABG suggests that the patient has a combination of both a respiratory component (as evidenced by the PaO2) and a metabolic component (as evidenced by the HCO3-).These two components combine to give acidosis - however the metabolic component has 'compensated' the respiratory acidosis, pushing the pH towards normality.This is because the kidneys have retained bicarbonate to try and retain base (raising the HCO3-), and the lungs have increased minute ventilation to drive off CO2 (lowering the PaCO2). This results in acidosis but with a relatively normal pH.The overall picture is one of respiratory acidosis which has been partially compensated by metabolic alkalosis.
